technique: line breaks — where the breath falls, and what the break withholds for a beat
lesson: Today we work on line breaks. A line break is the place where one line stops and the next begins, and it makes you pause for a beat before you get the next word. Look at where this poem breaks. "just a thing / asking to be lifted true and pinned." The break stops you after "a thing," so for one beat you don't know what the thing does. Then "asking" arrives. Same here: "animals that know / your step before the door." The break holds back "your step." You wait, then it lands. This works because the pause makes you lean toward the missing word. When it comes, you notice it more. Try this: write a sentence, then break the line one word before the most important word, so that word starts the next line. The second time through, listen for how the short lines near the end speed up before "So — up!" Here is the poem.
poem:
The gate hangs on one hinge still, caught half-swung
where you left it in last evening's failing hands—
not broken, not yet mended, just a thing
asking to be lifted true and pinned.
The fence line past it runs off into fog,
each post a question the gray morning keeps.
Somewhere down there a latch wants closing right,
a wire wants the pull of your two thumbs,
and the frost that stands on everything will go
soft and bead and run once you are out in it.
The barn breathes warm with animals that know
your step before the door, that count on it—

There are a few small things waiting that only you can close, and they'll feel good done—

So — up!
